deep_dive_html:
The High Cost of Forced Relocation

For dental practitioners, a relocation clause is not merely a logistical inconvenience; it is a potential practice-ending event. Unlike standard retail tenants, dental offices rely on highly specialized, permanent infrastructure, including complex plumbing, compressed air lines, specialized electrical loads, and lead-based X-ray shielding. When a landlord invokes a relocation clause to accommodate a larger anchor tenant or a building redevelopment, they are effectively forcing you to undergo a massive, unbudgeted capital expenditure.

Landlords often draft these clauses with extreme ambiguity, granting themselves the unilateral right to move you to any "comparable" space. However, "comparable" is a subjective term that can be exploited to move you to a space with inferior visibility, poor accessibility, or insufficient utility capacity. Without rigorous negotiation, you may find yourself responsible for the astronomical costs of decommissioning your current operatory and rebuilding a new one in a substandard location.

Securing Your Practice Infrastructure

To protect your investment, you must move beyond simple acceptance and implement aggressive defensive language. A sophisticated lease negotiation should focus on three non-negotiable pillars:

  • Total Cost Indemnification: The landlord must be contractually obligated to pay 100% of all costs associated with the move, including demolition, construction, permits, architectural fees, and the specialized installation of medical-grade utilities.
  • Strict Comparability Standards: The new premises must be functionally equivalent in terms of square footage, visibility, accessibility, and, most importantly, the ability to support your specific medical equipment and utility requirements.
  • Business Interruption Compensation: The lease must provide for rent abatement or direct compensation for any loss of revenue incurred during the period when the practice is unable to operate due to the relocation process.

If a landlord refuses to strike the relocation clause entirely, your fallback position must be a "consent-based" relocation, where the new space is subject to your absolute approval regarding its suitability for dental operations.
